name: Bianca Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the crew that looks after the industrial side of the network, out of the Riverside depot. So it's the lines feeding the factories and the warehouses in the business park, and the substations, the fenced yards with the big transformers that step the voltage down. A normal day might be a planned shutdown at a bottling plant at five in the morning so we can swap a switch while they're closed. I like the planning and the order of it, everything locked off and checked twice. What wears me out is the early starts and factory managers on the phone asking why it's taking so long.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into it, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I went to a trades open day at sixteen and a lineman let me try on a harness, and that was it. I've been mentoring apprentices the last five years, right now a young man called Kofi who's sharp but rushes. My husband Marek runs a roofing business with his brother, and we've got Petra, who's twelve, and Adam, who's nine. Mortgage, about four months saved, church on Sundays when the shifts allow. I use the AI now and then, to tidy up an incident report or help Petra with fractions, but I don't rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. It's a useful tool for paperwork and that's about it. I'd tell the apprentices to keep learning the real skills, because those are what count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a relief. My job, Marek's roofs, the apprentices I train, it all carries on. Maybe the reports get a bit quicker, which I wouldn't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Keep using the AI for reports now and then. Keep mentoring Kofi and keep putting a bit by each month for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal life, which suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Kofi. What do you mean, he rushes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month on a lock-off he went to test a line before I'd finished checking the earths. Nothing happened, but it could have. I sat him down after and told him, in this job the slow way is the only way home. He's good, he just needs to hear it a few more times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would AI be good for, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The incident reports, definitely. And the planning paperwork for shutdowns, the switching schedules. I'd still check every line of it myself. You don't sign something you haven't read.

S0.say: It's what she expected: a useful tool for paperwork and not much more. She'd tell apprentices to keep learning the real skills because those are what count.
S0.think: It's a relief because her job, Marek's roofing and the apprentices she trains all carry on. Faster reports would be welcome.
S0.do: Keeps working at the Riverside depot, using AI for reports now and then. Keeps mentoring her apprentice Kofi and putting a bit aside each month for the kids.
S0.feel: Calm, with normal life carrying on.
S0.quote: In this job the slow way is the only way home.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca values order, double-checking and passing skills on. She uses AI cautiously and insists on checking its work. Her role as a mentor is central to how she sees herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to stay competitive, so of course they'll use it, but they should keep training people properly. I'd say apprenticeships matter more, not less, when things change fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the planning side of my job gets taken over first, the switching schedules and the reports. That's the part I'm good at. So I'd be left with the hands-on part, and they might need fewer of us for that too. And I'd worry the company stops taking apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new planning software once the first crews had used it and it was proven. I'd ask to be part of training the apprentices on it, so I stay useful. At home, nothing dramatic, maybe put a bit more aside, fifty or a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing they're reorganising the depot. You wait to see where you land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the company stop taking apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're expensive for the first two years, and if software and machines are doing more, a manager might decide not to bother. That would be a mistake. You need people who understand the kit when the computer gets it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Marek's roofing business do in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roofs still need people on them, at least for now. Maybe the quoting gets done by AI, his brother would like that. I think they'd be alright for a good few years.

S1.say: Businesses have to stay competitive, so they'll use it, but they should keep training people properly. Apprenticeships matter more, not less, when things change fast.
S1.think: The planning side she's good at, like switching schedules and reports, would be taken over first, leaving the hands-on work where fewer people may be needed. She worries the company stops taking apprentices.
S1.do: Learns the new planning software once other crews have proven it and asks to train apprentices on it. Puts an extra fifty to a hundred a month aside.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like waiting to see where she lands after a depot reorganisation.
S1.quote: You need people who understand the kit when the computer gets it wrong.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry centres on losing the part of the job she's best at and on the apprenticeship pipeline. She accepts companies' right to compete but expects them to train people. She'd adopt tools once proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have a duty to their workers, not just their shareholders. Give notice, help people move. I'd also say families and churches need to pull together, because the government won't be quick enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be very worried. Two years, and robots doing roofs and substations? Then my job and Marek's business go at the same time. Four months of savings, a mortgage, two kids. And the apprentices I've trained would have nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back straight away: no holiday, the kids' activities down to one each, eat out never. Save everything. I'd help Marek with the books and quoting so the business runs lean for as long as it can. If it came to it, I'd lean on my parents and our church community, and take temporary help if I had to, but I'd keep looking for work every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd done everything right and it didn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: 'Done everything right and it didn't matter'. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I did the apprenticeship, worked hard, never missed a shift without a reason, saved what we could. That's what I was taught and what I teach Kofi. If a machine takes it all in two years, what do I tell him? That's what would really get to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' notice, what would you try to get done first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the mortgage down as much as we could and ask the company about a proper redundancy deal. Maybe look at a safety certificate, because someone's still going to have to sign off on things, at least at first. But two years is very little time.

S2.say: Companies have a duty to their workers, not just shareholders: give notice and help people move. Families and churches need to pull together because government won't be quick enough.
S2.think: Robots doing roofs and substations in two years would take her job and Marek's business at once, with four months saved and a mortgage. The apprentices she trained would have nowhere to go.
S2.do: Cuts back at once, dropping the holiday and limiting the kids to one activity each, and saves everything. Helps run Marek's business lean, leans on parents and church if needed, takes temporary help only if necessary and looks for work daily.
S2.feel: Alarmed, feeling she did everything right and it didn't matter.
S2.quote: If a machine takes it all in two years, what do I tell him?
S2.fieldNote: Her sense of fairness is hurt as much as her finances: she followed the rules she teaches. The household risk is double because her husband's business is exposed. She'd accept public help only reluctantly and temporarily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to get ready if they're sensible. Companies should keep training and give fair notice. People should save and learn something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could get a safety inspector's qualification in five years, so I'm the one checking that the robots' work is safe. That's still work for someone careful like me. Petra would be seventeen, Adam fourteen. Marek and his brother would have time to think too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the safety certificate next year, part-time, the company might pay half. Get the savings up toward six months. Talk to Petra about what she wants to study, and maybe save toward that instead of the bigger house we'd been talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's a lot, but I can see the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd give up the bigger house. How big a decision is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big for us. We'd been looking at places with a garden for Adam, he's football mad. But a bigger mortgage in front of something like this? No. The garden can wait. The kids' futures can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To finish his apprenticeship, because the skills matter, and to pick up the safety side as he goes. And to save from his first pay packet, which no young man wants to hear. I'll tell him anyway.

S3.say: Five years is enough for sensible people to get ready. Companies should keep training and give fair notice, and people should save and learn something new.
S3.think: She could earn a safety inspector's qualification in five years and be the one checking robots' work, which suits someone careful. Her husband and his brother would also have time to plan.
S3.do: Starts a part-time safety certificate next year, hoping the company pays half, and builds savings toward six months. Drops the bigger-house plan and saves toward Petra's studies instead.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, able to see the steps.
S3.quote: The garden can wait. The kids' futures can't.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her orderly nature into a plan. She gave up a long-held family plan without much hesitation. Her advice to her apprentice mixes trade skills with thrift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this properly. Keep apprenticeships going, let people retrain while working, and let businesses adapt. No need for panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be alright. I'd be 53, the kids grown or nearly. I'd move into safety inspection and maybe train the next generation of inspectors. The main worry is whether there's a next generation to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the safety certificate over a couple of years, then maybe an assessor qualification to teach it. Keep saving steadily. We might still buy the bigger house in a few years, if things look clear by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more settled than not. It feels like a long road with signposts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might still buy the bigger house. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'd wait till about 2030 and see. If my inspector job looks solid, and Marek's still busy, then maybe. If not, we stay put. I'm not going to decide that today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Petra and Adam to take from the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you keep learning and you look after each other. That's the same thing my parents told me, just with robots in it now. And I'd want them near home, I'd be lost if they moved away.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to do this properly: keep apprenticeships going, let people retrain while working and let businesses adapt, with no need for panic.
S4.think: She thinks she'd be alright, moving into safety inspection and maybe training future inspectors at 53. Her main worry is whether there will be a next generation to train.
S4.do: Takes the safety certificate over a couple of years, then an assessor qualification to teach it. Keeps saving steadily and waits until about 2030 before deciding on the bigger house.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more settled than not, like a long road with signposts.
S4.quote: The main worry is whether there's a next generation to train.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her steady approach and mentoring role give her a clear path. She defers big family decisions until the picture is clearer. Her values come straight from her parents and faith.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Marek's business and my job would go together. What would help is companies giving real notice and keeping apprenticeships open for the jobs that remain. And some short-term help for families, tied to looking for work or training, not a handout for nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the young ones. Everyone asks people my age about their mortgages. But Kofi's twenty and he's just starting. I'd want someone asking what we owe him.

headlineQuote: I'd feel like I'd done everything right and it didn't matter.
portrait: Bianca Novak is a 43-year-old lineworker who maintains substations and the lines feeding a business park, a careful planner who mentors apprentices and lives by double-checking. Her husband runs a roofing business with his brother, and they have two kids, a mortgage and about four months saved. She uses AI now and then but always checks its work, and she believes companies should compete but also train people and give notice. Fast AGI alarms her because her job and her husband's business would go together and the rules she teaches would stop mattering, while five or ten years give her a clear path into safety inspection.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her job and her husband's roofing business would go at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Real notice from companies, apprenticeships kept open for the jobs that remain, and short-term family help tied to looking for work or training.
